title: Storage explained: HDD vs SSD, partitions & file systems
monthTitle: PC Hardware & How Computers Work (A+ Core 1)
summary: Learn how computers store files for the long term: the difference between hard drives and solid-state drives, the shapes and connectors they come in, and how partitions and file systems turn a raw disk into usable drive letters.
objectives: Explain the difference between an HDD and an SSD and when each is used
Identify common drive form factors and connectors (2.5", M.2, SATA, NVMe)
Describe what a partition is and tell GPT apart from MBR
Match common file systems (NTFS, exFAT, FAT32, ext4) to the right job
Explain what formatting does and how a drive becomes a drive letter
View disks, volumes and partitions safely using built-in Windows tools

quiz.q: Which statement best describes an SSD compared with a traditional HDD?
options: It uses spinning platters and a moving read/write head
It stores data in flash memory with no moving parts and is much faster
It is always cheaper per gigabyte than an HDD
It can only be used for the operating system, never for files
quiz.why: An SSD uses flash memory chips with no moving parts, so it is far faster and more shock-resistant than an HDD, which relies on spinning platters and a mechanical head.

quiz.q: What does the RPM rating on a hard drive (HDD) tell you?
options: How fast the platters spin, which affects performance
quiz.why: RPM means revolutions per minute. Faster-spinning platters (e.g. 7200 RPM vs 5400 RPM) generally read and write data quicker on a mechanical HDD.

quiz.q: An M.2 NVMe drive is faster than a 2.5" SATA SSD mainly because:
options: It connects over the PCI Express bus instead of the slower SATA bus
quiz.why: NVMe drives talk to the system over the high-speed PCIe lanes, which carry far more data per second than the older SATA interface used by 2.5" SATA SSDs.

quiz.q: Which partitioning scheme supports drives larger than 2 TB and more than four primary partitions?
quiz.why: GPT (GUID Partition Table) is the modern scheme that handles drives over 2 TB and many partitions. The older MBR scheme is capped at 2 TB and four primary partitions.

quiz.q: Name the default file system Windows uses for its system drive, and give one reason it is chosen.
quiz.answer: NTFS, because it supports large files, security permissions, and journaling that helps recover from crashes.
quiz.why: NTFS is the standard Windows file system; its permissions and journaling make it reliable and secure for the operating system and most internal drives.

quiz.q: In one sentence, what does formatting a drive actually do, and why must you be careful?
quiz.answer: Formatting writes a fresh, empty file system onto a partition, which erases the data that was there, so you must always confirm you have selected the correct disk.
quiz.why: Formatting prepares a volume for use but wipes existing files, so picking the wrong disk in a tool like Disk Management or diskpart can destroy data permanently.

body_markdown:
## Why storage matters

Your computer has two kinds of memory. **RAM** is fast but forgets everything when the power goes off. **Storage** is the slower, permanent home for your operating system, programs, and files — it keeps your data even when the PC is switched off. On a helpdesk, you will swap drives, clone systems, and explain to users why their old PC "feels slow." Very often the answer is the drive.

## HDD vs SSD

A **hard disk drive (HDD)** stores data on spinning magnetic **platters**. A tiny mechanical arm with a read/write **head** moves across the platter to find your data. The platters spin at a fixed speed measured in **RPM** (revolutions per minute) — commonly 5400 or 7200. Because parts physically move, HDDs are slower, noisier, and more fragile, but they are **cheap and come in huge capacities**, which makes them great for bulk storage and backups.

A **solid-state drive (SSD)** stores data in **flash memory** chips. There are **no moving parts**, so it is dramatically faster, silent, cooler, and far more resistant to bumps. Swapping an old HDD for an SSD is the single biggest speed upgrade you can give most computers. The trade-off is a higher cost per gigabyte.

## Form factors and connectors

Drives come in different shapes (**form factors**) and use different connectors:

- **2.5\" SATA** — a small rectangular drive that connects with a **SATA** cable. Both HDDs and SSDs use this shape.
- **M.2** — a thin stick that plugs flat onto the motherboard. Pronounced "em dot two."
- **SATA vs NVMe** — the connector is only half the story. A 2.5\" SSD or some M.2 drives use the older **SATA** bus. Faster M.2 drives use **NVMe**, which runs over the high-speed **PCIe** lanes and is many times quicker.

## Partitions: GPT vs MBR

A raw drive is just empty space. A **partition** is a section of the drive treated as a separate unit. One physical disk can hold several partitions. The **partition table** records this layout, and there are two schemes:

- **MBR (Master Boot Record)** — older, limited to **2 TB** and four **primary** partitions.
- **GPT (GUID Partition Table)** — modern, supports huge drives and many partitions. Required for UEFI boot.

## File systems and formatting

A partition still needs a **file system** — the rulebook for how files are stored and named. Common ones:

- **NTFS** — Windows default; permissions, large files, journaling.
- **exFAT** — great for large external/USB drives shared between Windows and Mac.
- **FAT32** — old and simple; can't hold files over 4 GB.
- **ext4** — the common Linux file system.

**Formatting** writes a fresh, empty file system onto a partition — and erases what was there. Once formatted, Windows assigns a **drive letter** (like `C:` or `D:`) so you can use it.

## Viewing drives safely

You can inspect storage without changing anything. Open PowerShell and run these read-only commands:

```powershell
Get-Disk
Get-Volume
Get-Partition
```

You can also open **Disk Management** (`diskmgmt.msc`) for a visual map. The command-line tool **diskpart** can also list disks read-only:

```text
diskpart
list disk
list volume
exit
```

**Warning:** never run format, clean, or delete commands unless you are 100% sure of the disk number. Selecting the wrong disk wipes it permanently.

## Your task

Open PowerShell on your PC and run `Get-Disk`, then `Get-Volume`, then `Get-Partition`. Write down, for your main drive: is it an HDD or SSD, what file system does it use (look at the `Get-Volume` output), and what drive letter is it? Then open Disk Management (`diskmgmt.msc`) and confirm your findings visually — without changing anything.

slides.narration: Welcome back to Month One, Lesson Three. Today we cover storage, the permanent home for everything on a computer. By the end you'll know the difference between a hard drive and a solid-state drive, the shapes and connectors they use, and how partitions and file systems turn a blank disk into the drive letters your users see every day.

slides.title: Storage vs memory
bullets: RAM is fast but forgets when power is off.
Storage is permanent — keeps data when off.
Holds the OS, programs and your files.
A slow drive is often why a PC feels slow.
slides.narration: First, let's clear up a common mix-up. RAM is your computer's short-term memory; it's fast, but it forgets everything the moment the power goes off. Storage is the permanent home for your operating system, your programs, and your files. It keeps your data even when the machine is switched off. On the helpdesk, when a user says their PC feels slow, the drive is very often the reason.

slides.title: Hard disk drives (HDD)
bullets: Spinning magnetic platters plus a moving head.
Speed measured in RPM, like 5400 or 7200.
Mechanical, so slower and more fragile.
Cheap and very large — great for backups.
slides.narration: A hard disk drive, or H D D, stores data on spinning magnetic platters. A tiny mechanical arm with a read-write head moves across the platter to find your data. The platters spin at a set speed measured in R P M, revolutions per minute, commonly five thousand four hundred or seven thousand two hundred. Because real parts move, hard drives are slower and more fragile, but they're cheap and come in huge sizes, which makes them perfect for bulk storage and backups.

slides.title: Solid-state drives (SSD)
bullets: Stores data in flash memory chips.
No moving parts — fast, silent, tough.
Biggest speed upgrade for most old PCs.
Costs more per gigabyte than an HDD.
slides.narration: A solid-state drive, or S S D, stores data in flash memory chips. There are no moving parts at all, so it's dramatically faster, completely silent, and far more resistant to knocks. Swapping an old hard drive for an S S D is the single biggest speed upgrade you can give most computers. The only trade-off is that it costs more per gigabyte.

slides.title: Form factors & connectors
bullets: 2.5" SATA: small drive on a SATA cable.
M.2: a thin stick straight onto the board.
SATA bus is older and slower.
NVMe runs over fast PCIe lanes.
slides.narration: Drives come in different shapes, called form factors. The two-point-five-inch S A T A drive is a small rectangle that connects with a S A T A cable. An em dot two drive is a thin stick that plugs flat onto the motherboard. But the connector is only half the story. Slower drives use the S A T A bus, while the fastest em dot two drives use N V M e, which runs over the high-speed P C I e lanes and is many times quicker.

slides.title: Partitions: GPT vs MBR
bullets: A partition is a section of a drive; one disk can hold several.
Each partition can become its own drive letter.
MBR: old, max 2 TB, four primary partitions.
GPT: modern, huge drives, many partitions, UEFI boot.
slides.narration: A brand-new drive is just empty space. A partition is a section of that drive treated as a separate unit, and one physical disk can hold several partitions, which is why a single disk can show up as both a C drive and a D drive. There are two schemes that record this layout. M B R, the master boot record, is the old one, limited to two terabytes and four primary partitions. G P T, the GUID partition table, is the modern scheme that supports huge drives and many partitions, and it's required for UEFI boot, so any new system should use G P T.

slides.title: File systems
bullets: NTFS: Windows default, secure, journaled.
exFAT: best for big external/USB drives.
FAT32: old, can't hold files over 4 GB.
ext4: the common Linux file system.
slides.narration: Once a partition exists, it needs a file system, which is the rulebook for how files are stored and named. N T F S is the Windows default, with permissions and journaling that make it reliable. ex-FAT is best for large external or U S B drives shared between Windows and Mac. FAT thirty-two is old and can't hold a single file bigger than four gigabytes. And e-x-t four is the common file system over on Linux.

slides.title: Formatting & drive letters
bullets: Formatting writes a fresh, empty file system.
It erases whatever data was there.
Windows then assigns a drive letter (C:, D:).
Always confirm you picked the right disk.
slides.narration: Formatting is the step that writes a fresh, empty file system onto a partition, and that means it erases whatever was there before. After formatting, Windows assigns a drive letter, like C colon or D colon, so you can actually use it. Because formatting wipes data, you must always, always confirm you've selected the correct disk before you do it.

slides.title: Viewing drives safely
bullets: Use read-only PowerShell commands first.
Get-Disk, Get-Volume, Get-Partition.
Disk Management gives a visual map.
Never format or clean the wrong disk!
slides.narration: You can inspect storage without changing a thing. In PowerShell, run Get dash Disk, Get dash Volume, and Get dash Partition. These are read-only, so they're completely safe. You can also open Disk Management by running disk-mgmt dot m s c for a visual map. Just remember the golden rule: never run format, clean, or delete on a disk unless you are one hundred percent certain of the disk number.

bullets: HDD = spinning platters; SSD = flash, faster.
M.2 NVMe over PCIe beats 2.5" SATA.
GPT is modern; NTFS is the Windows default.

Task: run Get-Disk / Get-Volume and record yours.
